rationale: A wins because it gives the founder more usable story machinery: different protagonists, real proof gates, and honest caveats. A's “6,000 brands are now buying grocery ads through a company that isn't a grocer” is a sharper buyer-side lens than B's softer “Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app — what that says about retail media,” which drifts toward panel-topic fog. B is competent, but it smuggles in outside pegs like “Amazon's cashierless stores helped define” while A mostly keeps the inventions on a leash.
gaps_in_A: “A cart that watches what you put in it is now the grocery aisle's newest ad surface” overstates the cart/ad connection. The update says carts track items and Instacart has ads; it does not say carts are ad inventory.

“The prevailing belief in retail media is that ad revenue rides on top of a growing transaction base” may be true, but it is external context not supplied in the update and needs attribution before pitching.
“this beat has already seen fail twice” is a cute swipe with no supplied evidence. Good editor-brain, bad fact hygiene.
“Honestly weak as a time hook” is correctly disclosed, but it means the fourth angle still needs a second peg or named advertiser before it deserves outreach.
gaps_in_B: “Amazon's cashierless stores helped define” is an invented competitor frame. The update gives no Amazon comparison, and competitor pegs are where sloppy pitches go to die.
“core delivery growth fell to single digits” sharpens the fact too far. The update says grocery-delivery order growth slowed to single digits; “fell” and “core” add interpretation.
“category-wide budget shift” asks the 6,000-brand number to carry a market thesis by itself. B admits it needs benchmarks, which means the angle is not yet fully earned.
“Next step: journalist-fit-check” is premature. B itself says there is no live external peg; list-building before proof and peg-checking is how founders burn good names.
